planting.note: Scatter seed directly on cleared, sandy soil in fall so it can germinate with cool-season rains and overwinter as a low rosette.

directions: Scatter seed directly on cleared, sandy soil in fall so it can germinate with cool-season rains and overwinter as a low rosette before flowering March through May. This Texas coastal-plain and Rio Grande Plains endemic bears yellow rays flecked with maroon at the base, giving rise to its crown tickseed name, and its early pollen and nectar are valuable to emerging native bees and small butterflies. It thrives in the deep sandy soils typical of the middle and southern Texas Gulf Coast and reseeds readily once established. Avoid rich or heavily irrigated beds, which favor floppy growth over the compact form seen in the wild.

planting.note: Set plants or direct-sow into wet, sandy or peaty soil in spring and keep the root zone from drying out through establishment.

directions: Unlike the common annual tickseeds, this fleshy-leaved Florida endemic is a true fall-blooming perennial best planted where soil stays consistently moist, such as pond margins, low prairies, and the damp edges of marshes. It is found statewide except the far northern Panhandle and supplies a critical late-season nectar source for bees and migrating butterflies after most Gulf Coast wildflowers have finished. Set plants or direct-sow into wet, sandy or peaty soil in spring and keep the root zone from drying out through establishment. Once rooted it spreads slowly to form dense colonies that tolerate periodic standing water.

planting.note: Direct-sow around the last frost into open, sunny ground; leaving late-season heads intact lets it self-sow modestly.

directions: Direct-sow around the last frost into open, sunny ground in the narrow east Texas, western Louisiana, and southwest Arkansas corridor this bushy tickseed calls home. Its abundant golden-yellow daisy flowers bloom from late spring into summer and draw a steady stream of native bees, sweat bees, and small skippers. Because natural populations are limited and localized, this species is a genuinely underused option for Gulf South pollinator meadows that already lean on the far more common Coreopsis lanceolata and tinctoria. Deadheading extends bloom, while leaving late-season heads intact lets it self-sow modestly without becoming aggressive.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto lightly raked, moist soil in spring or fall; tolerates both a fall sowing for spring bloom and a spring sowing for summer color.

directions: Broadcast seed onto lightly raked, moist soil in spring or fall, since this Florida native tolerates both a fall sowing for spring bloom and a spring sowing for summer color. As the official state wildflower it is planted along Florida highways and low pinelands for its long parade of small yellow, brown-centered daisies that feed native bees and support skipper and sulphur butterfly larvae. It thrives in the humid, sandy soils common across the northern Gulf Coast and readily reseeds each year if some spent flower heads are left standing. Keep soil evenly moist during germination but avoid waterlogging once seedlings are established.

planting.note: Plant dormant tuberous roots two to three inches deep in fall so they can root through the cool season; seed germinates erratically and needs 60-90 days cold-moist stratification.

directions: Plant dormant tuberous roots two to three inches deep in fall so they can root through the cool season and emerge as one of the very first Texas wildflowers to bloom, often as early as late January in South Texas. The greenish-white to purplish-blue flowers open on wiry stems above finely divided foliage, then the whole plant vanishes underground by early summer to escape the heat, so it pairs well with later-emerging perennials in a mixed bed. It prefers well-drained sandy or calcareous clay soils typical of Texas prairies and needs minimal supplemental water even in a dry Gulf Coast winter. Its early pollen is an important resource for the season's first native bees.
